\paragraph{Why minimum intervention works.}
Restraint in downweighting outperforms aggressiveness.
In the 38.2\% of batches where $\aeff$ determines $\bstar$, the selected exponent is 4.9$\times$ lower than the ESS-only upper bound (\S\ref{sec:regime}), preventing unnecessary suppression of borderline samples ($q \approx 0.4$--$0.6$) that carry useful training signal.
This behavior is robust across contamination levels ($\aeff$-binding: 38.2\% at $\rho{=}0.4$, 33.4\% at $\rho{=}0.6$) and seeds (CV ${<}2\%$).
$\aeff$ correlates with the true batch-level real fraction at Pearson $r \approx 0.70$ across $B \in \{4, 8, 16\}$, with a conservative bias of $-0.03$ (Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_validation}).

\paragraph{Where the advantage manifests.}
The advantage appears entirely at evaluation (PPL 17.65 vs.\ 17.69 on human-authored text); training loss curves overlap (${\sim}1.4\%$ difference), consistent with reshaping the effective distribution rather than changing the optimization trajectory.
Part of the PPL gain may reflect distribution matching: downstream benchmarks (Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}) show 4 of 5 tasks with small negative $\Delta$ (sign-test $p \approx 0.19$, $N{=}5$), suggestive but not significant.
The aggregate mean $\bstar \approx 1.4$ as a fixed exponent yields PPL 17.693, no better than uniform, because it masks extreme per-batch heterogeneity (std $\approx$ 1.9, range $[0, 20]$); per-batch adaptation is essential.
